facts.text: Gay Street was named after Nicholas Ruxton Gay, a surveyor who mapped the area in the 1740s.
After the Civil War, banks, insurance firms, and light industries such as brush factories and tobacconists sprang up on Gay Street.
Because Gay Street escaped Baltimore's Great Fire of 1904, its historic commercial buildings survived while downtown was rebuilt.
The district showcases Victorian Eclectic, Beaux‑Arts, Italianate, and Romanesque façades, reflecting Baltimore's late‑19th‑century commercial style.
The 11‑acre Gay Street Historic District, listed in 2003, contains 34 contributing buildings bounded by North Gay, Fallsway, Low, and North Exeter.
In the late 1800s, Jewish immigrants established clothing and textile sweatshops, tailoring factories, tanneries, and furniture shops, turning Gay Street into a bustling working‑class hub.
